CA-04.001: cells are the basic units of cellular organisms. a cell membrane helps regulate exchanges between the cell and its surroundings. the cell uses ribosomes to assemble proteins, and its internal structures let different processes take place in the same small space. bacteria and archaea lack a membrane-bound nucleus. in most eukaryotic cells a nucleus encloses much of the genetic material. some specialized cells, including mature human red blood cells, lose their nucleus. mitochondria in eukaryotes and chloroplasts in plants and many algae descend from bacteria that became incorporated into ancestral cells. metabolism is the set of chemical reactions in which a cell transforms matter and uses or stores energy. multicellular organisms distribute some of this work among specialized cells and tissues. the cell diagram depicts one general form of animal cell. membranes, surface structures, organelles and dimensions vary widely. cell membrane metabolism
CA-04.002: in cellular life, deoxyribonucleic acid (dna) carries inherited information. its strands consist of linked units with four common kinds of bases. the bases occur in sequences, and complementary bases can pair so that each strand can guide the copying of the other. changes in base sequence are called mutations. recombination can rearrange existing variation. inheritance passes some of this information to new cells and to descendants, while genes and environments both influence how organisms develop. genes operate within cells and environments; they do not determine every trait independently. dna mutation
CA-04.003: the frequency of inherited variants can change across generations. one mechanism is natural selection. in a particular environment, individuals with different inherited traits can differ in how many descendants they leave. a variant contributing to greater reproductive success can become more frequent. frequency can also change by chance, especially in small populations. that process is genetic drift. mutation creates new variants, and gene flow moves variants between populations. shared features and genetic comparisons provide evidence for common ancestry. an advantageous trait in one environment can be costly in another. evolution has no fixed destination. several mechanisms can operate on the same population at once. natural selection genetic drift
CA-04.004: an ecosystem includes organisms and the parts of their surroundings with which they interact. in a food web, a link can trace matter and energy transferred when one organism consumes another. producers use light or chemical reactions to make organic material. consumers obtain material and energy by feeding on other organisms or their remains. energy enters and leaves local ecosystems. elements such as carbon and nitrogen can be recycled between living bodies, air, water and sediment. earth's biosphere comprises the regions where life occurs and includes many connected ecosystems. food webs are variable and interdependent, not simple linear chains. food web biosphere
CA-04.005: a genome is the full set of an organism's genetic information. a chromosome is an organized dna molecule with associated material. a gene is a region of dna whose information contributes to making a functional rna or protein. during protein synthesis, a ribosome reads the sequence in messenger rna in groups of three bases. these groups specify amino acids or signals, such as when to stop. other portions of a genome may influence when genes are used or have functions unrelated to making a protein. inherited variation can influence how traits develop. the influence can depend on other inherited variants and on conditions during life. the organization and interpretation of genomes vary among organisms; the genetic code has some exceptions. genome gene
CA-04.006: earth's cellular organisms maintain boundaries, exchange matter and energy with their surroundings, and carry information that can be inherited. across generations, populations can evolve. a characteristic shared by living populations need not be expressed by every individual. for example, individual animals that cannot reproduce remain living organisms. evidence from ancient rocks and from comparisons among living organisms helps researchers reconstruct some of life's history. how early chemical systems began to maintain themselves, reproduce with variation and evolve remains unsettled. scientists study several possible pathways; a demonstration that one step can happen leaves the whole historical sequence open. the archive describes observed properties of terrestrial life. an agreed universal definition and an independent extraterrestrial example are still missing. inheritance biosignature
CA-04.007: ribonucleic acid, or rna, is a family of molecules built from linked units. messenger rna can carry a copy of information from dna to a ribosome. other rnas help the ribosome read the message and assemble amino acids in sequence. some rnas take part in regulation or catalyze chemical reactions. an amino acid chain can fold into a shape that enables a protein's function. proteins can provide mechanical structure, carry molecules or accelerate reactions. changes in a chain or in its surroundings can change how it folds or functions. gene expression and protein assembly vary across organisms and cellular circumstances. this account introduces shared roles at the level needed to read later biology articles. ribosome enzyme
CA-04.008: in oxygen-producing photosynthesis, cells use light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide. water supplies electrons and oxygen is released. plants, algae and cyanobacteria carry out this process. the chloroplasts visible in the leaf micrograph are sites of photosynthesis in plant cells. during aerobic cellular respiration, cells transfer energy from organic compounds into forms that can support their work. oxygen accepts electrons at the end of a series of transfers. cells of photosynthetic plants also respire. other metabolic pathways enable living cells to obtain energy when oxygen is unavailable. this overview describes familiar pathways. some forms of photosynthesis do not release oxygen, and the availability and use of light and oxygen vary among environments. organic molecule aerobic
CA-04.009: microorganisms are organisms studied at scales that often require a microscope. they occur in multiple branches of life. bacteria and archaea each form major groups, while many other microscopic organisms are eukaryotes, with a different internal cell organization. among eukaryotes, many plants use light energy to make organic material. fungi obtain nutrients from material around them, and many decompose remains or associate with other organisms. animals are multicellular and acquire organic nutrients from other organisms or their products. ferns, mushrooms and fish illustrate some of these groups. microorganism describes scale and mode of observation. it is a different kind of category from a lineage. the portraits show examples from many distinct branches, and no one photograph defines a group. eukaryote decomposer
CA-04.010: biodiversity includes variation among individuals, among species and among ecosystems. different species rely on different features of their surroundings. a forest and a coral reef differ in habitat, structure and exchanges of matter and energy, even without counting individual organisms. a species becomes extinct if its last living members die. a species can also disappear from part of its former range while surviving elsewhere. human changes to land and oceans, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and introduced organisms can reduce local or global biodiversity. many species are poorly observed. estimates of threatened species and of losses depend on observation, definitions, date and the scope of the assessment. extinction habitat
